title: Early irrigation in Mesopotamia
summary: An irrigation canal more than 7,000 years old has been found at Choga Mami, 110 km east of Baghdad. In Mesopotamia, artificial irrigation became a key innovation as people moved into the floodplains, where they could not rely on rain alone. At first, farmers drew water from the Tigris-Euphrates river system onto their fields using small canals.

uncertainty.note: Early canal systems excavated at Choga Mami date to the Samarra period of the 6th millennium BCE, approximately 6000–5500 BCE.

as_recorded.calendar: Radiocarbon and archaeological chronology, years ago
as_recorded.value: An early irrigation canal (#3.19), over 7 kyr old, was discovered in Choga Mami

Artificial irrigation was a key innovation, which underwent significant improvement over time. At first, irrigation was conducted by siphoning water directly from the Tigris-Euphrates river system onto the fields using small canals

where.modern_name: Choga Mami, Diyala Governorate, Iraq (near Mandali)
where.historical_name: Choga Mami, Samarran agricultural settlement in eastern Mesopotamia; no unified state existed at this date

importance.justification: Artificial diversion of water transformed arid river floodplains into productive agricultural land, laying the economic foundation for the world's first cities and states.

related.because: The domestication of cereal crops led early farming communities into arid regions where agriculture required artificial water supply.
Managing complex canal networks generated food surpluses and centralized administrative institutions that formed early states.
